5eab83af.text: In 2016 the philosopher Shannon Vallor asked whether classical virtues can guide a hyper-technological future. Her book's subtitle names the goal: a future worth wanting. Her idea, in short: old virtues, adapted, can help us live well with new technology.

c890e377.text: Vallor's technomoral self-control means choosing, and ideally wanting, what helps us flourish. Online, that starts with attention.
c890e377.spoken: Vallor's technomoral self-control means choosing, and ideally wanting, what helps us flourish. Online, that starts with attention.

d14b9804.spoken: A person who masters this virtue decides consciously when to engage with screens, rather than reacting to automated alerts.

4579f721.text: Technochauvinism versus technomoral wisdom. This slide sets blind faith in technological fixes against wise discernment about human needs. Technochauvinism is the data journalist Meredith Broussard's term. On one side, Technochauvinism, also called solutionism. It's the uncritical belief that every human and social problem has a technological solution, code fix, or automated app. For example, giving a lonely, grieving teenager a conversational AI companion rather than fostering real-world human friendships. On the other side, Technomoral Wisdom, which is about human flourishing. It's the reflective capacity to discern which human goods require embodied presence, vulnerability, and sustained personal labor. For example, Tasha sitting at the foot of Zoe's bed, listening without screens, restoring the human bond that no algorithm can provide.
